The situation

I joined Voat about 4 months ago after a friend shared it with me, and I fell in love with the laid back, respectful, thoughtful community. People did not spam memes or flame each other, and even in the most divisive conflict I've seen on the site (the /v/beatingwomen thing) most everyone remained very cordial and polite, and sought to find mutual understanding. Contrasted with the general culture on reddit to which I was accustomed in a site like this, it was incredibly refreshing.

They say that reddit is falling to the same malady that afflicted so many other places on the internet before it, the Eternal September. Reddiquette was a modest attempt at alleviating it, but ultimately rediquette is seen as something of a joke on reddit for a number of reasons. While Voat is pretty awesome right now, we've seen several large influxes of users from reddit who, while most likely value the same things that I do about the community here, may eventually bring with them some of the same habits that many of us find distasteful from elsewhere on the net. Common wisdom states that it is inevitable that with a rise in popularity, shitposting will increase, nuance is drowned out in favor of extremism, and well-thought out discussions are hidden beneath an ocean of easily-consumed images.

Innovation

I believe that humans are uniquely adaptable creatures. We find solutions to the most frustrating challenges through creative imagination, dogged persistance, and often sheer luck. Those solutions which work are shared, and all of society benefits. I see the Eternal September not as an insurmountable problem, but a challenge that Voat is currently in a position to meet head on through experimentation and innovation.

Those who say it has all been tried before are likely the same sort who said man will never fly on a heavier than air machine, nor go to the moon. The wright brothers had a belief, and they tried different ways to make that belief into a reality. We aren't trying to overcome the common-sense wisdom about the immutable law of nature that nothing as heavy as a human can lift up into the sky; our challenge is something demonstrably much more malleable: human social behavior in a specific context which we all collectively have an ability to influence.

The way I see it, there are a few variables that can be changed:

  • Site design and mechanisms - another reason Voat is refreshing is the active development and trying out of new ideas on an experimental basis. There are likely many creative methods which may be attempted to promote a more functional and valuable experience for everyone. There is much reason to be optimistic here - and such technical innovation requires the most work and has likely the highest immediate payoff.

  • Site rules - rules against misconduct can be enforced by the authority of admins and moderators. This is a valuable process, and it requires constant vigilance and a well-trained moderation team to be effective with large numbers of people.

  • Community culture - this is where Voat really shines for the moment. I think if the culture can be carefully guided and reinforced, then it has the highest chance of success in deterring behavior that is debilitative to Voat and the value the community feels in our home on the web here.

As a user, my ability to influence the first two is limited, but I believe that we all collectively can influence the third variable.

The Agreement

Thus we have born the Civil Voaters' Agreement: the democratically authored non-binding voluntary social contract for Voat users.

Think of it sort of like reddiquette, but with a few distinct differences:

  1. Community authored/edited
  2. Regularly reviewed for updating by the community
  3. Implicitly invites conscious assent via signatures of agreement with the principles it describes, making supporters more likely to act in accord with the values it expresses.

The technical details are relatively straightforward. I've reviewed a few posts on the subject of voat culture and from those created a rough draft, v.0.1-Alpha of the Civil Voaters' Agreement. I'm seeking feedback on how it may be improved before released as a v.0.5-Beta. Anyone may then submit proposals for changes, and at a regularly held review process those proposals are voted on by the community in order to improve the agreement.

True that a democratic process such as this will permit a fluctuating culture to redefine the document - it is hoped that review and discussion, debate on changes will produce more thoughtful reflection and collectively voters may make intelligent choices. If this fails, the document is permissively licensed and all forks and past versions are promoted and supported by /v/VoatersAgreement, the subverse where the Agreement is primarily intended to be planned and discussed. I am optimistic however that broad support of the general principles that our current culture establishes in this document will be reinforced by those leading through example, continuing to demonstrate civility and promotion of high quality content, and support for everyone's right to express themselves.

Here's the initial release: Version 0.1-Alpha of the Civil Voaters' Agreement: https://voat.co/v/voatersagreement/comments/144868

Here's the rough roadmap I have planned for the development of the CVA: https://voat.co/v/voatersagreement/comments/144591

I've heard many stories where video gaming has impacted someone's life in one way or another. I remember a story about this girl being saved from suicide by Harvest Moon and it just amazed me how much I saw myself in it. I can count many times in my own life where video gaming either provided a safe haven from the bullshit going on in my life to impacting large decisions I made.

My example is a video game called Catherine. The story goes that a man named Vincent begins having horrific nightmares about climbing a block tower, which he knows if he falls, he will die. This happens right as Vincent's girlfriend of five years proposes and he begins having doubts and a new girl mysteriously comes into his life full force. The game will ask you many questions and allow you to make choices on how Vincent responds to people in the game. Your responses are recorded via a mysterious meter with red on the left and blue on the right.

Anywho, the game's basic underlying principle to me was that you need to decide what you want in life and own up to it. You can't just coast through life doing what people expect you to do, that you have to make your own way in life. And after I played that, I moved out of my parent's house and never looked back.

So I ask, what is your story?
Q: Have video games emotionally impacted you? How?
Any time I'm not surrounded by smoke grenades I feel like I'm in constant danger. Thanks a lot insurgency.

That's an interesting question. My initial thought was just of games that I've had an emotional connection to. In that instance, it's Xenoblade. Up until this point, I've never played a video game that left me feeling so closely connected to the characters and events that transpired. But your question seems more geared at games that actually altered a view. I've read a few books that did that but overall I think my largest lesson from video games has been patience and a willingness to leave things unfinished. The example I'm considering is Metroid Prime. I invested tons of time into the game, made it to the final boss, and tried for a long while to make it through that fight. Eventually, I just lost interest but still felt compelled to enter into the battle. I never did beat it and had to reach a spot where I could accept defeat.

Two games come to mind: Photopia and Every Day the Same Dream.

Photopia: http://ifdb.tads.org/viewgame?id=ju778uv5xaswnlpl

Every Day the Same Dream: http://www.molleindustria.org/everydaythesamedream/everydaythesamedream.html

Both of these games elicited an extreme emotional response in me. Both are short, playable in a single sitting. Photopia probably is best experienced in the standalone .exe version, but it doesn't seem to work with newer versions of windows.

Both games are perhaps more story-like than tradtitional games. Still they require participation from the player, so I think they qualify.

I can't really express too much about them without spoiling them in case you decide to play them. I'll reiterate that each is entirely playable in a single sitting. They are very well-made, in my opinion.

I don't think I have been heavily emotionally impacted by any game in particular, but the people I've met in mmo's definitely helped me get through some tough times. It was nice to come home and know there would be friends wanting to play together when I went online.

I played competitive Team Fortress 2 for a while. I practiced every day. Read all the literature on the subject there was at the time. And even started to write some of my own. I was obsessed. I lived and breathed that game. Everything else in life was a distraction and in my way. It felt so good to carry my team. It felt even better when my team was doing well, and while I didn't carry, I was among them, filling my role above expectations.

As you can imagine, other areas of my life suffered tremendously. I had little social life. Didn't talk to girls. And could have been doing better in school.

I had this internal conflict. The life I was currently living, and the life I wanted in my future, they were not going to meet. Every day my inner turmoil became stronger and I was having less and less fun playing. I started going to the gym. I started flirting with girls. I did my homework. I retired from playing. But then I came back. I knew too much. I was too good. I couldn't throw it away.

I bounced back and forth, again and again, until one day it just clicked. I didn't touch the game. I didn't even miss it. I prevented myself from playing video games at all. Weeks passed. Months passed.

I'm now much more satisfied with my life and the direction it's going. I've only recently started playing video games again. I still have the standards of a hardcore player. But I no longer have the urge to play nor the time sink, of a hardcore player. My time spent playing video games on that level is a fond memory, but I hope I never go back.

Two. First one is Shadow of the Collossus. I cry every time i play that game, since it kinda mirrored what was happening in my real life. Not really hot on sharing that story, but it was almost like a religious experience to me.

Second one was MGS3. I think it was the first and last time i hesitated , and damn did I jump when I did.

SoC was amazing, looking back at it, I can point at its flaws, and be more critical but I still hold memory of when I completed the game. The credits were rolling and my body and mind just kinda sat there for a good moment, I didn't even realize I had a controller in my hand, no movie/book/game had ever hit me like SoC did.

If theories about dreams being a way to sift through life problems subconsciously are true then videogames can probably help people do something similar if they're used in moderation. I also wouldn't be suprised if videogames, sports, and politics let people experience a part of themselves which gets supressed into their unconscious through societal conditioning. On the other hand, since we've evolved too far from our natural environments to permanently return back to them, videogames often give people a visual replacement for nature while supressing other senses. This is why I also think it would be interesting to see what stimulating one sense too much, at the expense of others, does to our brains, bodies, and emotions.

It's taken me long enough how to figure this out. It's simple. It's really simple. STOP WASHING YOUR HAIR EVERYDAY. I have fine, very curly hair. It's always dry. In the summer, it's worse. I'm of the pasty pale variety but it gets frizzy enough to give Diana Ross and her iconic hair a run for her money.

Going no-poo made me realize what I was missing. Oil.

The more frequent you wash, the less likely the oils are able to move from your scalp to your ends. The curls make it more difficult for oil to migrate as opposed to straight hair. Eventually, I went back to shampoo but I use significantly less and I wash about 2 to 3 times a week as opposed to everyday. I still shower daily, I just keep my hair up when it isn't a shampoo day.

At times my hair does get a bit greasy so I do two things: 1. I use a boars hair brush to help redistribute the oil. I bought mine at Bed, Bath, and Beyond and it was about $12. 2. I apply corn starch to my roots. It makes a good dry shampoo replacement. Sometimes I add ground up lavender to add a nice scent.

All in all, now my hair is much more manageable and I no longer need use multiple products in my hair just to simply control it. Just keep it simple.
PSA: Don't wash your hair everyday
